docs.title: Categorical Foundations: Weaknesses, Vulnerabilities, and Threats
docs.text:
A central contribution of the CSA taxonomy is its formal separation of Weaknesses, Vulnerabilities, and Threats, resolving pervasive terminological confusion across the AI industry.

Weaknesses represent intrinsic design attributes, inductive biases, and statistical limitations inherent to probabilistic neural models. Examples include the inability to separate instructional prompts from untrusted data in natural language contexts, tendency toward hallucination when sampling outside training distributions, and susceptibility to floating-point rounding variations. Weaknesses are mathematical properties of the architecture rather than bugs.

Vulnerabilities denote actionable control deficiencies and exploitable states in software runtimes, deployment pipelines, configuration baselines, or access models. These flaws allow an adversary to trigger an underlying weakness. Examples include exposing unauthenticated tool invocation endpoints, failing to sanitize RAG database entries, using unencrypted prompt caches, or granting unconstrained network egress to an inference container.

Threats represent active adversary tactics or adverse operational events that exploit Weaknesses or Vulnerabilities to achieve malicious goals. Threats encompass deliberate campaigns such as automated jailbreak fuzzing, indirect prompt injection delivered via untrusted web documents, training set poisoning, model parameter extraction, etc.

docs.title: The Four Pillars of the Taxonomy
docs.text: The CSA taxonomy structures the security landscape around four interconnected pillars: System Assets, Service Lifecycle, Impact Categories, and Threat Categories.

docs.title: Pillar 1: System Assets
docs.text:
The framework classifies enterprise LLM systems into five distinct asset clusters, establishing clear ownership boundaries across engineering teams:

  1. Data Assets: The core knowledge inputs, parameters, and telemetry powering the system. This cluster includes pre-training text corpora, supervised fine-tuning records, external RAG (RAG) knowledge stores, metadata data cards recording provenance and consent, active user session histories, prompt inputs, generated output tokens, internal weight matrices, training hyperparameters, and operational audit logs.
  2. LLM-Ops Environment: The underlying physical and cloud infrastructure supporting system execution. This tier comprises distributed training clusters, inference endpoints, application hosting runtimes, multi-cloud interconnects, identity and access management (IAM) perimeters, network ingress controllers, and long-term cloud object stores housing model weights.
  3. Model: Beyond stored model weights (covered in Data Assets above), the CSA defines the model through its architectural structure, its specialization level (base foundational versus fine-tuned models), its distribution mode (model file versus API access), and its model card [4], which records training lineage, ownership, and testing baselines.
  4. Orchestrated Services: Middleware components that intermediate between foundation models, auxiliary microservices, and external systems. Assets include response caching layers, specialized LLM security gateways, automated deployment pipelines, continuous monitoring services, runtime optimization engines (such as quantization and weight pruning routines), security plugins, and general agent execution loops handling planning and tool dispatch.
  5. AI Applications: Downstream, user-facing software products delivering generative and agentic capabilities to humans or automated workflows.

docs.title: Pillar 2: The Six-Stage Service Lifecycle
docs.text:
Drawing upon ISO/IEC 5338, the taxonomy decomposes an LLM service into six sequential phases. Each stage introduces specific security requirements and defensive obligations:

  1. Preparation: Engineering teams source training datasets, establish ethical and legal collection criteria, and execute data curation. Curation includes deduplication, filtering, anonymization, and labeling. Teams provision hardware resources (GPUs and TPUs), configure storage with verifiable chain-of-custody tracking, and assemble multidisciplinary teams spanning ML engineers, software developers, domain specialists, and privacy officers.
  2. Development: The functional model is constructed from prepared data and computational infrastructure. Activities encompass architecture selection (transformer layer depth, attention mechanisms), hyperparameter tuning, framework selection (PyTorch, TensorFlow, Ray), iterative gradient training, and tokenization. Primary considerations include training transparency, explainability, computational resource efficiency, and strict artifact version control to ensure complete build reproducibility.
  3. Evaluation and Validation: Prior to operational release, the model undergoes exhaustive testing. Teams compute quantitative metrics (perplexity, task accuracy, BLEU scores) and gather qualitative human judgments of fluency and relevance. This stage mandates bias and fairness audits, real-world generalization testing, human-in-the-loop review, and adversarial Red Teaming to discover jailbreaks and boundary failures. Re-evaluation routines monitor for data drift (shifting real-world input distributions) and model drift (declining task prediction quality) after deployment, establishing empirical triggers for model retraining.
  4. Deployment: Validated models are integrated into production environments. Workflows use containerization, auto-scaling architectures, and Infrastructure as Code (IaC) to guarantee repeatable deployments. Engineers harden the AI supply chain across external agent protocols and third-party plugins, implementing runtime guardrails such as input classifiers, prompt injection defenses, output sanitizers, and PII filters.
  5. Delivery: This operational phase encompasses steady-state maintenance, real-time logging, telemetry ingestion, performance monitoring, security incident response, and structured feedback collection. Maintenance schedules govern defect remediation, library patching, base model version tracking, and planned downtime communications. Continuous improvement cycles use feedback loops to refine hyperparameters and test newer candidate architectures.
  6. Service Retirement: When a model becomes obsolete, redundant, or legally untenable, it undergoes formal decommissioning. Teams archive model weights, software configurations, and audit records in compliance with enterprise retention schedules. Personal and sensitive data is purged across training and session stores to satisfy data governance mandates such as GDPR and CCPA. Finally, organizations perform cryptographically secure disposal of model artifacts and physical media sanitization (shredding or degaussing) to eliminate residual recovery risks.

docs.title: Pillar 3: Impact Categories and the Extended CIA Triad
docs.text:
The taxonomy anchors consequence evaluation in the classic Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability triad, while incorporating modern extensions from NIST AI 100-2:

  • Loss of Confidentiality: Unauthorized exposure of intellectual property, model weights, training corpora, proprietary system instructions, or sensitive user session data through extraction attacks, inversion techniques, or unauthenticated log storage.
  • Loss of Integrity: Intentional or accidental corruption of training weights, fine-tuning data, retrieval context, or generated model outputs. Compromised integrity results in biased predictions, misleading information, or attacker-controlled responses that undermine system trust.
  • Loss of Availability: Interruption of inference endpoints, exhaustion of API rate limits, computational memory starvation, or infrastructure failure preventing legitimate access to the generative service.
  • Loss of Privacy: Unauthorized extraction of personal identity attributes or inferential profiling derived from training memorization or session histories.
  • Abuse/Misuse: Weaponization of model capabilities for automated cyberattacks, social engineering, disinformation campaigns, or unauthorized autonomous actions.

docs.title: Pillar 4: The Nine Threat Categories
docs.text:
The taxonomy groups adversarial attack surfaces and operational hazards into nine discrete threat categories:

  1. Model Manipulation: Evasion techniques, direct prompt injections, and indirect prompt injections embedded in external content that manipulate model reasoning, override safety filters, or coerce the system into generating illicit outputs.
  2. Data Poisoning: Injection of malicious, falsified, or biased samples into pre-training corpora, fine-tuning datasets, or retrieval databases. Poisoning implants persistent backdoors or skews classification boundaries, degrading model trustworthiness.
  3. Sensitive Data Disclosure: Unauthorized exposure of proprietary corporate documents, personal data, or secret credentials processed by the service. Disclosure occurs via model memorization extraction, unintended caching, or insecure output generation.
  4. Model Theft: Unauthorized extraction, distillation, parameter estimation, or reverse engineering of proprietary models. Competitors or threat actors replicate intellectual property without incurring the underlying capital training expenditure.
  5. Model Failure and Malfunctioning: Unplanned operational degradation resulting from software defects, unhandled runtime exceptions, hardware memory faults, hallucinated outputs, or undetected concept drift.
  6. Insecure Supply Chain: Vulnerabilities introduced through third-party foundation models, untrusted pre-trained checkpoints, compromised software dependencies (such as malicious PyPI or npm packages), or hardware components.
  7. Insecure Applications and Plugins: Flaws within tool interfaces, client software wrappers, or third-party extensions. Vulnerabilities permit unauthorized privilege escalation, insecure output handling, or downstream command injection in connected host environments.
  8. Denial of Service (DoS): High-volume request flooding, complex recursive queries, or computational sponge attacks designed to consume disproportionate memory and compute resources, rendering the service unavailable.
  9. Loss of Governance and Compliance: Inability to demonstrate regulatory adherence, maintain traceable audit records, satisfy compliance mandates (such as the EU AI Act), or enforce internal safety policies, resulting in severe financial and legal liabilities.

docs.title: Role in Purple Teaming
docs.text:
Purple teams use the CSA LLM Threats Taxonomy to replace fragmented, ad-hoc prompt testing with structured, lifecycle-aware validation exercises. Instead of treating LLMs as standalone black boxes at the application layer, collaborative operators assess risk across all four taxonomy pillars.

During exercise scoping, the Red Team references the nine threat categories to develop comprehensive adversary emulation plans. Operators simulate real-world attack chains: crafting indirect prompt injections embedded in retrieval stores (Threat 1), submitting high-dimensional extraction queries to evaluate model distillation risks (Threat 4), and testing whether manipulated plugin parameters achieve unauthorized command execution (Threat 7).

In response, the Blue Team uses the asset classification and lifecycle breakdown to position layered defensive controls. Defensive engineers place security gateways ahead of inference endpoints to detect anomalous token distributions, deploy strict schema validation on tool integration boundaries, and establish continuous monitoring for model drift.

By conducting joint validation across preparation, development, deployment, and live delivery phases, Purple teams uncover structural gaps that traditional web application assessments overlook.

docs.title: Mapping to SCF C|P-RMM
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, a Vulnerability is directly associated to Control Deficiencies (an absent, failing, or misconfigured security control). This definition is broad enough such that it must encompass both CSA’s Weaknesses (intrinsic statistical and architectural constraints of neural networks) and CSA’s Vulnerabilities (implementation states or configuration errors that can be exploited).

To put it another way, certain model hardening techniques (such as input sanitization, adversarial training, or model constitutions) can be seen as the implementation of security controls of the LLM, and hence an absence or failure of those techniques (which translates to a CSA Weakness) can be considered a SCF C|P-RMM Vulnerability.

docs.title: Critique
docs.text:
The CSA LLM Threats Taxonomy provides an essential, holistic foundation for securing generative ML systems. Its primary strength lies in its comprehensive lifecycle scope. By grounding security in ISO/IEC 5338 processes from initial preparation through service retirement, the taxonomy prevents organizations from focusing solely on runtime inference while ignoring upstream data poisoning and downstream decommissioning liabilities. Furthermore, its formal distinction between mathematical Weaknesses, software Vulnerabilities, and operational Threats brings much-needed precision to risk discussions.

The framework’s primary architecture centers around single-model request-response pipelines and conversational applications. While it acknowledges general agents under Orchestrated Services, it lacks detailed threat modeling for autonomous multi-agent environments. Emergent risks such as inter-agent protocol exploitation, automated delegation chains, and decentralized agent marketplaces require specialized companion frameworks such as CSA MAESTRO to achieve complete architectural coverage.

docs.title: CSA MAESTRO
docs.text: This section details the Cloud Security Alliance Multi-Agent Environment, Security, Threat, Risk, & Outcome framework (CSA MAESTRO). [1] [2]

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The CSA MAESTRO framework is a specialized threat modeling methodology published by the Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) in 2025. It addresses the architectural and operational realities of autonomous agent systems and multi-agent environments.

Classical threat modeling frameworks, such as STRIDE [3], PASTA [4], and LINDDUN [5], were designed for deterministic software architectures where code execution paths, system boundaries, and user privileges are static. When applied to autonomous agent systems, these traditional models encounter clear limitations:

  • Non-Deterministic Execution: Agents make probabilistic planning choices, making deterministic boundary tracking ineffective.
  • Autonomous Agency: Agents initiate tool invocations, decompose objectives, and write intermediate scripts without direct human review.
  • Multi-Agent Dynamics: Complex ecosystems involve peer agents communicating, collaborating, or competing, introducing risks like inter-agent collusion, identity spoofing, and cascading failure states.

MAESTRO organizes threat modeling around a seven-layer reference architecture, isolating the specific risks and defense surfaces present at each tier of the system.

docs.title: The Seven-Layer Reference Architecture
docs.text:
The MAESTRO framework decomposes agentic systems into seven functional layers, spanning underlying compute infrastructure up to consumer-facing agent marketplaces.

Layer Architecture Tier Primary Function Distinct Threat Manifestations Layer 7 Agent Ecosystem Public and private agent registries, marketplaces, and user integration endpoints. Rogue agent listings, marketplace rating tampering, agent impersonation, identity hijacking, and tool misuse. Layer 6 Security and Compliance Cross-cutting vertical governance, guardrail agents, and policy enforcement engines. Guardrail evasion, security agent data poisoning, credential theft, regulatory non-compliance, and defense model extraction. Layer 5 Evaluation and Observability Benchmarking suites, telemetry collectors, audit logs, and anomaly detection pipelines. Metric manipulation, telemetry tampering, logging denial of service, alert evasion, and sensitive data leakage in traces. Layer 4 Deployment and Infrastructure Container runtimes, cloud hosts, microVM sandboxes, and orchestration platforms. Container escape, orchestration tampering, Infrastructure-as-Code injection, host resource hijacking, and lateral movement. Layer 3 Agent Frameworks Runtime orchestrators, execution toolkits, prompt pipelines, and client libraries. Vulnerable library dependencies, missing input validation on tool arguments, backdoor triggers, and framework API denial of service. Layer 2 Data Operations Vector databases, RAG pipelines, cache stores, and semantic memory. Persistent state poisoning, vector retrieval manipulation, data exfiltration from context stores, and embedding tampering. Layer 1 Foundation Models Base language models, multimodal reasoning engines, and fine-tuned checkpoints. Adversarial perturbations, model extraction, training data poisoning, backdoor triggers, and computational sponge attacks.

docs.title: Cross-Layer Threat Vectors
docs.text:
While individual layers possess specific security boundaries, MAESTRO stresses that high-consequence attacks in agentic environments routinely cross architectural boundaries:

  1. Supply Chain Propagation: An adversary compromises an open-source tool library in Layer 3 (Agent Frameworks), using it to bypass memory controls in Layer 2 (Data Operations) and hijack high-level tasks in Layer 7 (Agent Ecosystem).
  2. Infrastructure-to-Memory Lateral Movement: Exploiting a container configuration defect in Layer 4 (Infrastructure) permits unauthorized read access to the vector store in Layer 2 (Data Operations), exposing internal tenant retrieval indices.
  3. Cascading Goal Misalignment: Poisoned retrieval data in Layer 2 induces faulty reasoning in Layer 1 (Foundation Models), causing the primary agent to emit corrupted sub-tasks that derail coordinating peer agents across the broader Layer 7 ecosystem.

docs.title: Architectural Threat Patterns
docs.text:
MAESTRO formalizes recurring threat configurations across common operational deployments:

  • Single-Agent Deployments: Risk concentrates around goal manipulation and unbounded autonomous execution loops where missing human confirmation gates enable unauthorized financial or data operations.
  • Multi-Agent Collaborations: Risk centers on unauthenticated communication channels, agent identity spoofing, and distributed deadlocks where peer agents misinterpret reciprocal message payloads.
  • Task-Oriented Integrations: Risk manifests through parameter injection and denial-of-service floods targeting backend API endpoints called by the agent during task execution.

docs.title: Role in Purple Teaming
docs.text:
Purple teams use the CSA MAESTRO reference architecture to systematically evaluate cross-layer security boundaries in autonomous systems. Rather than treating an AI deployment as a monolithic service, the Red Team executes multi-tier attack paths across MAESTRO’s seven layers, while the Blue Team verifies whether intermediate security controls detect and contain the progression.

During collaborative exercises, operators test whether compromises at lower architectural tiers can cascade into higher-level agent coordination. For example, the Red Team attempts to exploit a vulnerable dependency in Layer 3 (Agent Frameworks) to access sensitive embeddings in Layer 2 (Data Operations) or manipulate registration states in Layer 7 (Agent Ecosystem). In response, the Blue Team deploys layer-specific guardrails, including microVM execution sandboxes in Layer 4 and cryptographic signature verification on inter-agent messages in Layer 6. Retesting these vectors ensures that a localized failure at one tier does not compromise the broader agentic ecosystem.

docs.title: Mapping to SCF C|P-RMM
docs.text: Mapping CSA MAESTRO to the SCF C|P-RMM framework aligns the layer-specific threats, technical vulnerabilities, and operational impacts against standard risk definitions.

docs.title: 1. Adversary Actions as Threats
docs.text: In SCF C|P-RMM, a Threat represents the external entity or event capable of causing harm. MAESTRO’s threat landscape catalogs these active vectors: malicious prompt injection payloads, rogue agents registered in marketplaces, adversarial sponge inputs, and intercepted inter-agent communication channels.

docs.title: 2. Architectural Flaws as Control Deficiencies
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, a Vulnerability is strictly defined as a Control Deficiency (an absent, failing, or misconfigured defense).

MAESTRO’s seven layers directly identify the control deficiencies enabling an attack:

  • Layer 3: Missing parameter schema validation on client tools.
  • Layer 2: Absence of write-integrity verification on vector database embeddings.
  • Layer 4: Unconstrained container privileges allowing host filesystem access.
  • Layer 7: Unauthenticated agent registry discovery endpoints permitting malicious agent registration.

docs.title: 3. Operational Outcomes as Realized Risk
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, Risk represents the quantifiable or qualitative consequence of a threat exploiting a control deficiency (\(\text{Risk} = \text{Threat} \times \text{Vulnerability} \times \text{Impact}\)).

MAESTRO captures this realization through operational outcomes: financial exhaustion from uncontrolled token consumption, exfiltration of private customer records from semantic memory, and corrupted business decisions resulting from compromised multi-agent consensus.

docs.title: Critique
docs.text:
The CSA MAESTRO framework provides an indispensable structural foundation for threat modeling Agentic AI Systems. By breaking down monolithic model deployments into seven distinct layers, it separates base model vulnerabilities from orchestration, data pipeline, and infrastructure exposures. This clear separation helps engineering teams assign defensive responsibilities across specialized platform, data, and security teams.

However, the rapid evolution of agent communication standards continues to shift how tools, client orchestrators, and host runtimes interface. Security practitioners must routinely update their layer boundaries to ensure emerging protocol specifications are accurately mapped within the reference architecture.

---

docs.title: FIRST Common Vulnerability Scoring System
docs.text: This section details the FIRST Common Vulnerability Scoring System (FIRST CVSS), maintained by the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams (FIRST). [1], [2]

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The FIRST Common Vulnerability Scoring System is an open, industry-standard framework used to communicate the technical characteristics and severity of software and hardware vulnerabilities. Rather than assigning subjective priority labels, FIRST CVSS produces a composite vector of categorical metric values that resolve into a deterministic numerical score between 0.0 and 10.0.

FIRST CVSS is the universal baseline for vulnerability disclosure programs, the National Vulnerability Database (NVD), and security advisory management.

docs.title: Metric Groups and Structural Architecture
docs.text:
The scoring system categorizes vulnerability metrics into distinct operational groups:

  1. Base Metrics: Capture the intrinsic qualities of a vulnerability that remain constant over time and across user deployment environments. Base metrics assess the attack surface, execution prerequisites, and direct impact on system security attributes.
  2. Threat Metrics (formerly Temporal Metrics): Measure factors that evolve during the vulnerability lifecycle, such as exploit code availability, proof-of-concept weaponization, and active exploitation in the wild.
  3. Environmental Metrics: Quantify the impact of the vulnerability within a specific organization’s infrastructure, factoring in compensating security controls and the criticality of the affected system to business operations.

docs.title: Evolution Across Specification Revisions
docs.text: FIRST CVSS has evolved through multiple major revisions to improve mathematical rigor, curb score inflation, and adapt to modern distributed software architectures.

docs.title: Version 2.0: Architectural Baseline
docs.text: Published in June 2007, FIRST CVSS version 2.0 established the formal division between Base, Temporal, and Environmental metric tiers. It introduced early equations for intermediate Exploitability and Impact sub-scores, evaluating Access Vector, Access Complexity, Authentication, and Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability impacts scored as None, Partial, or Complete.

docs.title: Version 3.0 and 3.1: Scope and Refinements
docs.text:
Published in December 2015, FIRST CVSS version 3.0 added the Scope (S) metric to identify whether a compromised authority affects resources outside its security boundary. Version 3.0 introduced the concept of Privileges Required (PR), separating authorization barriers from Attack Complexity (AC), and adopted the RoundUp ceiling function.

FIRST CVSS version 3.1, released in June 2019, preserved identical scoring equations to version 3.0 while refining terminology. It clarified that Attack Complexity measures conditions beyond attacker control (such as race conditions or specific timing windows), standardized the treatment of shared software libraries, and eliminated ambiguities in Scope transitions.

docs.title: Version 4.0: The MacroVector Paradigm
docs.text:
Published in November 2023, FIRST CVSS version 4.0 restructured the standard to curb score inflation and capture complex architectures:

First, it replaced the monolithic Base-Temporal-Environmental inheritance model with four standalone nomenclature classes: - CVSS-B: Base metrics only. - CVSS-BT: Base and Threat metrics. - CVSS-BE: Base and Environmental metrics. - CVSS-BTE: Base, Threat, and Environmental metrics.

Second, version 4.0 retired the single Scope metric and separated system impacts into two explicit targets: - Vulnerable System Impact: Measures direct Confidentiality (VC), Integrity (VI), and Availability (VA) consequences within the software or service hosting the flaw. - Subsequent System Impact: Measures secondary Confidentiality (SC), Integrity (SI), and Availability (SA) consequences inflicted upon external systems reached through the compromised vulnerable system.

Third, version 4.0 separated prerequisite deployment conditions from exploit difficulty by introducing Attack Requirements (AT) alongside Attack Complexity (AC).

Fourth, version 4.0 moved away from single continuous algebraic equations. It maps metric combinations into six Equivalence Classes (EQ1 through EQ6) to form a 6-digit MacroVector (such as 001200), determining baseline scores through pre-computed lookup tables and non-linear interpolation.

docs.title: Qualitative Severity Classifications
docs.text:
Under versions 3.0, 3.1, and 4.0, numerical scores map to qualitative severity ratings:

Numerical Score Range Qualitative Severity Rating 0.0 None 0.1 – 3.9 Low 4.0 – 6.9 Medium 7.0 – 8.9 High 9.0 – 10.0 Critical

docs.title: Role in Purple Teaming
docs.text:
Purple teaming uses FIRST CVSS as a shared language between offensive operators and defensive engineers. During collaborative exercises, the Red Team executes exploit chains against identified software flaws, while the Blue Team verifies detection telemetry in Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) systems and Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) platforms. Scoring flaws with standardized CVSS vectors enables both teams to evaluate whether defensive monitoring reliably alerts on the specific attack vectors and privilege transitions exploited during the exercise.

The framework guides joint prioritization when analyzing chained attack paths. If an offensive operator exploits a CVSS 9.8 Critical flaw to bypass external perimeter boundaries, the Blue Team can deploy compensating controls, such as web application firewall rules or network microsegmentation, to break the chain before vendor patches are published. Retesting the scenario confirms whether these interim defenses successfully prevent lateral progression.

The Environmental Metric Group is the primary calibration mechanism in Purple Teaming. Software vendors publish Base scores assuming a worst-case scenario: complete internet exposure and zero defensive controls. In an enterprise exercise, Blue engineers provide data on existing compensating controls, while Red operators attempt to circumvent them. Environmental metrics (formalized as CVSS-BE and CVSS-BTE in version 4.0) adjust the baseline score based on those empirical results. A flaw rated Medium globally escalates to Critical if Red proves that internal network segmentation fails. Conversely, a Critical flaw drops in severity if Red confirms that Blue’s network isolation prevents remote access.

docs.title: Automated Scoring With the Gurple Agent Skills
docs.text:
Gurple provides an automated scoring skill in .agents/skills/calculate-cvss to streamline assessments across CVSS versions 2.0, 3.0, 3.1, and 4.0.

For installation and management procedures via npx skills, see the skills README.

docs.title: Mapping to SCF C|P-RMM
docs.text: To map the FIRST Common Vulnerability Scoring System to the SCF C|P-RMM framework, one must examine how FIRST CVSS differentiates between technical flaws, threat interactions, and resultant harm.

docs.title: 1. Quantifying Control Deficiencies
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, a Vulnerability is defined as a Control Deficiency (an absent, failing, or inadequately configured defensive mechanism).

FIRST CVSS is the industry standard to evaluate the severity of that deficiency. Base metrics, such as Privileges Required, Attack Requirements, and Attack Complexity, quantify the architectural weakness that allows a control failure to occur.

docs.title: 2. Threat Exploitability Versus Realized Risk
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, Risk is the consequence of a Threat successfully exploiting a Vulnerability (\(\text{Risk} = \text{Threat} \times \text{Vulnerability} \times \text{Impact}\)).

FIRST CVSS reflects this exact tripartite model: - The Exploitability metric group evaluates the accessibility and operational overhead required for a Threat actor to reach the vulnerability. - The Threat metric group in version 4.0 assesses active exploit maturity and weaponization in the threat environment. - The Impact metric groups (VC/VI/VA and SC/SI/SA) measure the magnitude of harm inflicted when the flaw is exploited, directly representing the realization of Risk.

docs.title: Critique
docs.text: The FIRST Common Vulnerability Scoring System is an indispensable pillar of modern cybersecurity, providing an objective, vendor-neutral baseline that drives patch management and regulatory compliance worldwide. Its mathematical structure eliminates arbitrary human impressions, while version 4.0’s separation of Vulnerable and Subsequent system impacts brings needed clarity to multi-tier enterprise architectures.

docs.title: Structural Limitations in Artificial Intelligence and Contrast With OWASP AIVSS
docs.text:
Despite these strengths, applying FIRST CVSS directly to GenAI, LLMs, and autonomous agent loops exposes critical architectural limitations:

  • Non-Deterministic Execution: FIRST CVSS assumes deterministic software behavior. LLMs operate probabilistically, meaning prompt injections manipulate semantic context rather than binary execution paths.
  • Agent Autonomy Blind Spot: FIRST CVSS ignores the autonomy of agents. A command injection flaw receives the same base score whether running in a developer sandbox or in an autonomous agent with unmonitored host access.
  • Emergent Impact Modalities: FIRST CVSS struggles with AI-specific harm. Flaws like Denial of Wallet, recursive task spawning, and memory poisoning cause severe financial and operational damage without server downtime.
  • Artificial Severity Ceilings: Standard API isolation forces prompt injections into Medium severity due to low technical privileges, even when they completely redirect the agent’s core business mission.

These gaps demonstrate that FIRST CVSS Base scores establish an empirical floor for deterministic software vulnerabilities. Capturing compound agentic risk in non-deterministic systems requires an agent-centric standard, explored later in this chapter: the OWASP Artificial Intelligence Vulnerability Scoring System (OWASP AIVSS).

---

docs.title: MITRE ATLAS™
docs.text: This section details the MITRE Adversarial Threat Landscape for Artificial-Intelligence Systems (MITRE ATLAS™). [1]

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: MITRE ATLAS™ is a publicly accessible, living knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques based on real-world AI incident observations. As AI systems become more popular, ATLAS provides a much-needed complement to the traditional MITRE ATT&CK® framework, focusing explicitly on the unique vulnerabilities and attack vectors specific to ML and GenAI.

docs.title: Tactics
docs.text:
A Tactic represents the “why” of an ATLAS™ technique. It is the adversary’s tactical objective: the reason for performing an action.

MITRE ATLAS™ includes 16 distinct Tactics:

ID Title AML.TA0000 AI Model Access AML.TA0001 AI Attack Staging AML.TA0002 Reconnaissance AML.TA0003 Resource Development AML.TA0004 Initial Access AML.TA0005 Execution AML.TA0006 Persistence AML.TA0007 Defense Evasion AML.TA0008 Discovery AML.TA0009 Collection AML.TA0010 Exfiltration AML.TA0011 Impact AML.TA0012 Privilege Escalation AML.TA0013 Credential Access AML.TA0014 Command and Control AML.TA0015 Lateral Movement

docs.title: Techniques
docs.text: A Technique represents “how” an adversary achieves a tactical goal by performing an action. For instance, Discover AI Model Family (AML.T0014) is a Technique under the Discovery (AML.TA0008) Tactic.

docs.title: Mitigations
docs.text:
A Mitigation is a security concept or technology that can be implemented to prevent or detect the successful execution of a Technique. For instance, Use Ensemble Methods (AML.M0006) is a Mitigation for Discover AI Model Family (AML.T0014).

A single mitigation can apply to multiple techniques, and a single technique can be countered by multiple mitigations.

docs.title: MITRE ATLAS™ Matrix
docs.text:
The MITRE ATLAS™ Matrix [2] is a view of the framework that organizes the Tactics and Techniques into a matrix, and may be used to identify and prioritize security controls. Each column is a Tactic, and each row is a Technique. By clicking through a Technique, one is able to access lists of Mitigations and Procedure Examples.

An alternative perspective is to think of the framework as a 3-dimensional matrix combining Tactics (x-axis), Techniques (y-axis), and Mitigations (z-axis). Each element in this matrix forms a tuple of (Tactic, Technique, Mitigation), as seen in Figure 1.

Figure 1: 3D view of the MITRE Atlas™ Matrix.

In Figure 1, an element of the matrix is highlighted, which is the tuple:

(Tactic, Technique, Mitigation) = (AML.TA0008, AML.T0014, AML.M0006)

where

ID Title AML.TA0008 Discovery AML.T0014 Discover AI Model Family AML.M0006 Use Ensemble Methods

Most tuple combinations are nonexistent due to the hierarchical nature of the framework, making the matrix highly sparse. Although imperfect, the 3D perspective is useful to simplify the complex structure that the navigation of the original MITRE ATLAS™ Matrix presents.

docs.title: Role in Purple Teaming
docs.text:
In ML and AI operations, Purple Teaming uses the MITRE ATLAS matrix to structure threat emulation against non-traditional attack surfaces. Because classical endpoint security tools cannot detect adversarial perturbations or semantic prompt manipulation, the Red Team executes specific ATLAS techniques—such as model inversion, evasion via crafted inputs, or training data extraction—while the Blue Team evaluates specialized AI telemetry.

This joint testing validates whether ML guardrails, semantic firewalls, and vector database logging alert on active tampering. When the Red Team submits structured query sequences designed to reconstruct model parameters (AML.T0024) or extract confidential system instructions, the Blue Team observes inference telemetry to identify behavioral deviations. The exercise produces an empirical AI coverage scorecard, directing engineering efforts toward implementing targeted mitigations (such as input perturbation filtering or differential privacy bounds) and retesting to confirm that defensive controls successfully neutralize the technique.

docs.title: Mapping to SCF C|P-RMM
docs.text:
The mapping of MITRE ATLAS™ Tactics and Techniques to the SCF C|P-RMM framework follows the exact same structure as discussed in the MITRE ATT&CK® section.

The MITRE ATLAS™ Tactic called Impact (AML.TA0011) directly represents the realization of the Risk in SCF C|P-RMM.

docs.title: Critique
docs.text:
MITRE ATLAS™ is heavily anchored in traditional ML (ML) attacks, such as Data Poisoning, Model Evasion, and Model Inversion. For organizations building modern applications by strictly wrapping commercial Large Language Model (LLM) APIs, many of these ML-specific techniques are entirely out of scope, relying on the model provider to address them. This can make the framework feel overwhelming or overly complex for teams focused solely on GenAI application security.

---

docs.text: [1] “MITRE ATLAS™.” https://atlas.mitre.org/. [2] “ATLAS Matrix MITRE ATLAS™.” https://atlas.mitre.org/matrices/ATLAS.

docs.title: MITRE ATT&CK®
docs.text: This section details the MITRE Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge (MITRE ATT&CK®). [1]

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The MITRE ATT&CK® framework is arguably the industry standard for modeling traditional enterprise cyber threats. It provides a comprehensive matrix that classifies offensive actions taken by threat actors across various domains, such as Enterprise IT, Mobile, and Industrial Control Systems (ICS).

docs.title: Tactics
docs.text: A Tactic represents the “why” or the tactical objective of an adversary. It represents the reason for performing an action. Examples include Initial Access, Execution, and Privilege Escalation.

docs.title: Techniques
docs.text: A Technique represents “how” an adversary achieves a tactical goal. For instance, achieving the tactic of Initial Access might involve the technique of Phishing or Exploiting Public-Facing Applications. Techniques are often further divided into Sub-techniques for more granular descriptions of attacker behavior.

docs.title: Mitigations
docs.text: Mitigations are defensive concepts or mechanisms used to prevent or detect the execution of a technique.

docs.title: Role in Purple Teaming
docs.text:
Purple teams rely on the MITRE ATT&CK matrix as the primary operational framework for threat emulation and detection engineering. Instead of conducting uncoordinated penetration testing, the Red Team designs exercises around specific adversary techniques—such as exploiting public-facing applications or abusing command interpreters—while the Blue Team inspects detection telemetry in real time.

This collaborative dynamic allows engineers to identify and close visibility gaps across the enterprise. When the Red Team executes a technique, Blue observers verify whether endpoint sensors and security information and event management (SIEM) systems generate actionable alerts. The joint team tracks assessment outcomes across the matrix to establish a measurable detection scorecard: classifying each technique as blocked by preventative controls, detected through logged telemetry, or unmonitored. Blue engineers then author targeted detection rules, and the Red Team re-executes the procedure to validate alert fidelity.

docs.title: Mapping to SCF C|P-RMM
docs.text: To map the concepts of MITRE ATT&CK® to the SCF C|P-RMM framework, one must align how each framework views the attacker versus the defense.

docs.title: 1. Tactics and Techniques Map vs. Threats
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, a Threat defines the “person or thing likely to cause damage”. MITRE ATT&CK® is essentially a detailed catalog of those sources of damage.

Tactics (the adversarial goal) and Techniques (the specific execution) represent the granular aspects of the Threat. When a malicious actor executes a Technique against a system, that is the literal materialization of the Threat in the SCF framework.

docs.title: 2. Mitigations vs. Controls
docs.text: Mitigations describe the precise security Controls needed to stop an attack.

docs.title: 3. The Realization of Risk
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, Risk is created when a Threat exploits a Vulnerability.

When an adversary successfully executes a specific Technique because the system lacks the corresponding Controls (Mitigations were not implemented), the resulting damage is the Risk.

The MITRE ATT&CK® Tactic named Impact (TA0040) directly represents the realization of the Risk in SCF C|P-RMM.

docs.title: Critique
docs.text:
MITRE ATT&CK® is heavily tailored toward generic endpoints, networks, and cloud infrastructure. When developing Large Language Model (LLM) applications or Agentic workflows, conventional tactics like lateral movement through active directory or exploiting OS-level vulnerabilities often do not capture the unique cognitive and application-level manipulations used against GenAI systems. Therefore, MITRE ATT&CK® must be used in conjunction with GenAI-focused frameworks such as MITRE ATLAS™ and OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications to provide a comprehensive view of GenAI threats.

---

docs.title: References
docs.text: [1] “MITRE ATT&CK®.” https://attack.mitre.org/.

docs.title: MITRE CAPEC™
docs.text: This section details MITRE Common Attack Pattern Enumeration and Classification (MITRE CAPEC™). [1]

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: MITRE CAPEC™ is a comprehensive catalogue of known attack patterns employed by adversaries to exploit known weaknesses. Attack patterns describe the common mechanisms, approaches, and methods adversaries use to compromise a system.

docs.title: Hierarchical Relationships
docs.text: Attack patterns are organized hierarchically. At the highest abstraction level, Categories group patterns sharing common characteristics. These cascade down into abstract Meta patterns, and finally into highly specific Standard and Detailed patterns focused on a particular execution methodology.

docs.title: Anatomy of an Attack Pattern
docs.text: When examining a specific attack pattern—such as Identity Spoofing (CAPEC-151)—the framework provides a structured decomposition of the adversary’s approach. Each entry specifies execution prerequisites, required attacker resources, and typical likelihood ratings alongside operational impact consequences. Direct mappings connect the pattern to underlying software flaws in MITRE CWE™ and specify actionable defensive mitigations.

docs.title: Role in Purple Teaming
docs.text:
Purple teams use MITRE CAPEC to deconstruct attack patterns into granular execution stages that can be tested and defended incrementally. Because CAPEC documents the specific prerequisites, resource requirements, and step-by-step methodologies used by adversaries, the Red Team can construct precise, reproducible test cases rather than relying on ad-hoc exploit payloads.

During Purple Team engagements, Blue engineers use CAPEC’s attack flow breakdowns to position inspection points across each phase of an attack. When the Red Team executes a multi-step pattern, the Blue Team evaluates whether intermediate filters—such as input validation gateways or authentication boundaries—detect the initial probing before exploitation completes. Retesting confirmed attack patterns ensures that defensive controls address the underlying behavioral pattern rather than an isolated signature.

docs.title: Mapping to SCF C|P-RMM
docs.text: To map the concepts of MITRE CAPEC™ to the SCF C|P-RMM framework, one must align the methodology of an attack with the exploitation of a system’s defenses.

docs.title: 1. Attack Patterns vs. Threats
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, Risk materializes when a Threat successfully exploits a Vulnerability (a control deficiency).

MITRE CAPEC™ essentially catalogs the methodologies and mechanisms of precisely how that exploitation occurs. An Attack Pattern describes the exact process a Threat actor uses to exploit a specific Vulnerability (which is often defined by a MITRE CWE™).

docs.title: 2. Mitigations as Controls
docs.text: Just as SCF C|P-RMM relies on Controls to mitigate Vulnerabilities, each CAPEC Attack Pattern provides specific, actionable Mitigations. These recommendations correspond directly to the technical, operational, and architectural controls necessary to eliminate the control deficiency.

docs.title: 3. Consequences as Realized Risk
docs.text: In SCF C|P-RMM, Risk represents the quantifiable or qualitative damage that occurs when a threat exploits a control deficiency (\(\text{Risk} = \text{Threat} \times \text{Vulnerability} \times \text{Impact}\)). The Consequences cataloged across CAPEC patterns—such as unauthorized data disclosure, system state corruption, or administrative privilege loss—represent the realization of that organizational risk.

docs.title: Critique
docs.text:
Like most MITRE frameworks, MITRE CAPEC™ was primarily developed with traditional enterprise software, web applications, and network infrastructure in mind. While it accurately maps broad concepts like “Injection” or “Data Manipulation,” it often lacks the specialized depth required to natively model highly nuanced GenAI and Large Language Model (LLM) vectors, such as complex semantic prompt injection or model jailbreaking. Consequently, while CAPEC remains an excellent conceptual resource for understanding fundamental attack mechanics, securing modern agentic applications necessitates using it in conjunction with GenAI-focused frameworks like MITRE ATLAS™ and OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications.

---

docs.title: References
docs.text: [1] “CAPEC - Common Attack Pattern Enumeration and Classification (CAPEC™).” https://capec.mitre.org/index.html.

docs.title: MITRE CWE™
docs.text: This section details MITRE Common Weakness Enumeration (MITRE CWE™). [1]

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The MITRE CWE™ is a community-developed list of common software and hardware weakness types. A “weakness” is a condition in a software, firmware, hardware, or service component that, under certain circumstances, could contribute to the introduction of vulnerabilities.

A 2025 CWE Top 25 list has been published by MITRE, providing a very useful view of the most common and dangerous weaknesses, as of 2025.

docs.title: Weaknesses vs. Vulnerabilities
docs.text: In the MITRE CWE™ framework, a Weakness is an underlying flaw (e.g., inadequate input validation), while a Vulnerability is a specific occurrence of that weakness in a particular product (often tracked as a Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, or CVE).

docs.title: Hierarchical Structure
docs.text: MITRE CWE™ weaknesses are organized hierarchically. Pillars represent the most abstract weaknesses, which are broken down into Classes, then into Base level weaknesses, and finally into specific Variants. For example, the abstract concept of Improper Neutralization cascades down into granular variants like SQL Injection or Cross-Site Scripting (XSS).

docs.title: Role in Purple Teaming
docs.text:
Purple teams use MITRE CWE to anchor security testing in root-cause flaw validation rather than superficial symptom mitigation. During joint assessments, the Red Team designs targeted exploit scenarios against specific weakness classifications—such as deserialization flaws (CWE-502) or improper input validation (CWE-20)—while the Blue Team audits static application security testing (SAST) rule coverage and runtime application defenses.

This collaboration ensures that engineering fixes eliminate the foundational software defect. When the Red Team successfully exploits a weakness, developers often deploy simple string filters that an attacker can easily bypass. In a Purple Team exercise, the Blue Team verifies that remediation addresses the underlying CWE class through structural controls, such as parameterized queries, strict schema validation, or safe serialization formats. The Red Team then re-tests the modified code path to verify that the entire weakness category has been neutralized.

docs.title: Mapping to SCF C|P-RMM
docs.text: To map the concepts of MITRE CWE™ to the SCF C|P-RMM framework, one must align how each framework views systemic flaws and defensive gaps.

docs.title: 1. Weaknesses Map to Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, a Vulnerability is strictly defined as a Control Deficiency (a missing, ineffective, or failing defense).

The MITRE CWE™ provides a specific, standardized vocabulary to describe these very Control Deficiencies at a technical level. Therefore, instances of a CWE (a Weakness) represent the underlying technical flaws that directly constitute a Vulnerability in the SCF framework.

docs.title: 2. The Role in Realizing Risk
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, Risk is the result of a Threat exploiting a Vulnerability.

While frameworks like MITRE ATT&CK® catalog the Threats (the “who” and “how” of the attack), MITRE CWE™ catalogs the Vulnerabilities (the gaps being exploited). Without the presence of a CWE (Weakness/Vulnerability), the Threat cannot successfully materialize into actual Risk.

docs.title: Critique
docs.text:
The MITRE CWE™ is comprehensive and provides the taxonomic foundation for many other security frameworks, including standard application security scanners. However, because it originated in traditional software engineering, it often approaches GenAI weaknesses abstractly. For instance, Prompt Injection is typically mapped to the broader concept of Improper Neutralization of Directives in Dynamically Evaluated Code (CWE-95), which fails to articulate the nuanced, semantic nature of LLM manipulation.

---

docs.title: NIST AI 100-2 E2023
docs.text: This section details the National Institute of Standards and Technology Special Publication AI 100-2e2023: Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations (NIST AI 100-2 E2023). [1]

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Published in January 2024 as part of the NIST Trustworthy and Responsible AI series, NIST AI 100-2 E2023 establishes a foundational taxonomy and terminology for Adversarial Machine Learning (AML). The publication surveys modern adversarial research, establishing a formal conceptual hierarchy that covers predictive algorithms, deep neural networks, and generative language models.

Rather than cataloging isolated software bugs, the publication organizes adversarial machine learning across three fundamental dimensions: attacker goals, attacker capabilities, and lifecycle stages.

docs.title: Core Taxonomy Dimensions
docs.text: The taxonomy structures adversarial machine learning across three interdependent dimensions that dictate how attacks are constructed and evaluated.

docs.title: 1. Attacker Goals and Objectives
docs.text:
NIST categorizes adversarial objectives into four primary security properties:

  • Integrity Violations: The adversary forces the model to produce incorrect predictions chosen by the attacker (targeted) or arbitrary erroneous outputs (untargeted), while preserving normal performance on benign inputs to avoid detection.
  • Availability Violations: The adversary degrades overall model utility or throughput. In generative architectures, this includes computational sponge attacks that maximize token generation latency, exhausting server GPU memory.
  • Confidentiality Violations: The adversary extracts proprietary information about model parameters, architecture, or internal latent representations (model stealing and model extraction).
  • Privacy Violations: The adversary infers whether specific sensitive records were included in the training dataset (membership inference) or reconstructs private training data verbatim (data extraction).

docs.title: 2. Attacker Capabilities and Knowledge
docs.text:
NIST establishes three distinct threat actor profiles based on access levels:

  • White-Box: The attacker possesses complete knowledge of the target system, including model weights, network architecture, training loss functions, activation values, and gradient data.
  • Black-Box: The attacker interacts with the system exclusively through inference queries, observing only emitted text or probability distributions without internal visibility.
  • Gray-Box: The attacker holds partial knowledge, such as the pre-training dataset distribution or model family, but cannot inspect internal runtime states or fine-tuned parameter weights.

docs.title: 3. Lifecycle Attack Stages
docs.text:
Adversarial interventions target two operational phases of the ML lifecycle:

  • Training and Development Phase: Attacks manipulate data collection, data preparation, or model fine-tuning. This stage encompasses data poisoning, where attackers inject malicious records into training sets, and backdoor attacks, where models are trained to associate specific trigger tokens with malicious behaviors.
  • Testing and Inference Phase: Attacks occur after deployment. Attackers submit crafted inputs (adversarial examples or prompt injections) designed to evade filters, trigger backdoors, or extract private information without altering model weights.

docs.title: Generative AI and Large Language Model Threat Taxonomy
docs.text:
Section 3 of the report provides a detailed classification of threats specific to generative models:

Section Attack Classification Threat Mechanism Typical Impact Section 3.1 Data Poisoning in Fine-Tuning Adversaries inject corrupted samples into pre-training corpora, instruction-tuning datasets, or reinforcement learning feedback loops. Compromised safety alignments, systematic political or corporate bias, and embedded latent backdoors. Section 3.2 AI Supply Chain and Deserialization Attackers publish compromised open-source models packaged in unsafe serialization formats like Python pickle files. Arbitrary code execution (RCE) on the host machine during model weight loading. Section 3.3.1 Direct Prompt Injection Attackers craft input prompts that overwrite system prompt constraints and bypass developer instructions. Unauthorized model behavior, jailbreaking, and execution of prohibited tasks. Section 3.3.2 Indirect Prompt Injection Adversarial instructions reside in untrusted third-party data sources (web pages, customer emails, documents) retrieved by the model. Data exfiltration, unauthorized API calls, and persistent semantic context manipulation. Section 3.4 Model Inversion and Training Extraction Attackers repeatedly query language models with structured prefixes to trigger memorized sequences. Reconstruction of proprietary source code, personal identifiable information (PII), and confidential training text.

docs.title: Mitigation Strategies in NIST AI 100-2
docs.text:
NIST identifies technical defenses across each lifecycle phase:

  • Training Defenses: Applying differential privacy algorithms during optimization, filtering web corpora for synthetic anomaly patterns, and computing cryptographic hashes over training checkpoints.
  • Format Hardening: Replacing unsafe execution-capable serialization formats with secure, read-only weight containers such as Safetensors.
  • Inference Defenses: Employing perplexity filters, output guardrails, and input sanitization to detect adversarial text sequences before they reach model context windows.

docs.title: Role in Purple Teaming
docs.text:
Purple teams use the NIST AI 100-2 E2023 taxonomy to calibrate adversarial testing across realistic attacker knowledge tiers and lifecycle stages. Because ML defenses vary substantially depending on what an adversary can access, the Red Team constructs exercises around specific threat profiles—testing black-box prompt extraction through public APIs or gray-box evasion against known foundation model families—while the Blue Team measures defensive efficacy.

This collaborative approach allows organizations to test both pre-deployment and runtime safeguards. During an exercise, the Red Team attempts to bypass input sanitizers and perplexity filters using obfuscated prompt injections, or probe fine-tuned models for training data leakage. The Blue Team evaluates whether runtime guardrails alert on adversarial token sequences and inspects output filtering policies to prevent sensitive text disclosure. Retesting against evolving attacker knowledge levels ensures that defensive controls remain effective even if internal model details leak.

docs.title: Mapping to SCF C|P-RMM
docs.text: The formal taxonomy of NIST AI 100-2 E2023 maps directly to the SCF C|P-RMM model by distinguishing attacker mechanisms from system weaknesses and operational damages.

docs.title: 1. Adversary Profiles and Attacks as Threats
docs.text: In SCF C|P-RMM, a Threat represents the external entity or action capable of inflicting damage. NIST’s knowledge tiers (White-Box, Gray-Box, Black-Box) model the threat actor’s capability, while specific attack techniques (Direct Prompt Injection, Data Poisoning, Sponge Attacks) represent the actionable threat vectors.

docs.title: 2. Architectural Gaps as Control Deficiencies
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, a Vulnerability is strictly defined as a Control Deficiency (an absent, failing, or inadequately configured defensive mechanism).

NIST identifies these exact deficiencies: * Ingesting uncurated web scrape data without anomaly detection represents a data validation control deficiency. * Using unencrypted, unverified model serialization formats represents a software supply chain integrity deficiency. * Granting models direct access to external web content without strict delimiter separation represents an input boundary control deficiency.

docs.title: 3. Taxonomical Objectives as Realized Risk
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, Risk is the consequence of a Threat exploiting a Vulnerability (\(\text{Risk} = \text{Threat} \times \text{Vulnerability} \times \text{Impact}\)).

NIST’s four attacker objectives correspond directly to organizational risk categories: * Integrity Risk: Flawed medical diagnoses, fraudulent automated approvals, or corrupted decision telemetry. * Confidentiality and Privacy Risk: Regulatory non-compliance and exposure of proprietary source code or confidential user records. * Availability Risk: Compute exhaustion, excessive cloud billing, and production application downtime.

docs.title: Critique
docs.text:
The primary contribution of NIST AI 100-2 E2023 is its scientific rigor. By anchoring modern generative AI vulnerabilities in established adversarial machine learning theory, the publication avoids the marketing hype that frequently distorts commercial security discussions. Its precise distinctions between attacker knowledge (White-Box vs. Black-Box) and attack lifecycles (training vs. inference) provide an objective foundation for enterprise risk assessment.

However, organizations applying NIST AI 100-2 must confront an essential technical constraint documented within the report:

Unlike classical cybersecurity vulnerabilities, where code patches can provide deterministic remediation, many generative AI attack surfaces lack complete theoretical defenses. In particular, prompt injection stems from the fundamental lack of mathematical separation between control instructions and data in natural language architectures. As NIST documents, current defenses are heuristic and empirical, functioning to elevate attacker cost rather than providing guaranteed security boundaries. Security teams must therefore design defense-in-depth controls around the model rather than expecting model weights to defend themselves.

---

docs.title: NIST AI 100-2 E2025
docs.text: This section details the National Institute of Standards and Technology Special Publication AI 100-2e2025: Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations (NIST AI 100-2 E2025). [1]

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Published in March 2025 as a finalized Special Publication, NIST AI 100-2 E2025 supersedes the earlier NIST AI 100-2 E2023 draft report. The publication establishes a formal, operationalized catalog for Adversarial Machine Learning (AML), transitioning exploratory research into an actionable baseline for enterprise threat modeling and risk management.

While the 2023 edition established foundational concepts, the 2025 edition introduces structural additions designed to integrate with automated vulnerability management pipelines and federal compliance frameworks.

docs.title: Primary Structural Differences Between E2023 and E2025
docs.text:
The 2025 edition introduces four major structural evolutions over the 2023 release:

Assessment Dimension NIST AI 100-2 E2023 NIST AI 100-2 E2025 Taxonomy Taxonomy Indexing Referenced attacks through generic section numbers (such as Section 3.2 or Section 3.3). Establishes the formalized NISTAML machine-readable identification system (such as NISTAML.018:2025). Model Categorization Blended classical deep learning algorithms with emerging generative models across continuous sections. Explicitly bifurcates the threat landscape into Predictive AI (PredAI) and Generative AI (GenAI) architectures. Framework Integration Positioned primarily as an academic survey of literature and conceptual terminology. Directly maps adversarial attack classes and technical mitigations into the four core functions of the NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage). Mitigation Pragmatism Cataloged theoretical defense proposals from academic ML papers. Evaluates operational feasibility, explicitly documenting the absence of mathematically complete defenses for prompt injection.

docs.title: Predictive AI Versus Generative AI Threat Surfaces
docs.text:
NIST AI 100-2 E2025 establishes a clear operational boundary between two fundamentally distinct paradigms:

  • Predictive AI (PredAI): Systems designed for classification, regression, and detection tasks (such as fraud detection models or medical imaging classifiers). Attacks against PredAI center on mathematical optimization techniques, such as adding imperceptible adversarial noise (Fast Gradient Sign Method or Projected Gradient Descent) to shift feature vectors across decision boundaries, or poisoning training labels to degrade accuracy.
  • Generative AI (GenAI): LLMs and multimodal foundation architectures that generate dynamic, unstructured content. Attacks against GenAI exploit the semantic conflation between developer control instructions and user data, targeting conversational reasoning loops, retrieval context, and external tool execution.

docs.title: The NISTAML Taxonomy Catalog
docs.text:
The central innovation of the 2025 edition is the NISTAML numbering system. This schema provides unique, unambiguous identifiers that security operations centers, vulnerability registries, and automated scanners can reference directly:

NISTAML Identifier Attack Classification Target Modality Operational Mechanism NISTAML.010:2025 Data Poisoning PredAI & GenAI Injecting malicious samples or tainted instruction-tuning records into pre-training corpora or RLHF preference sets. NISTAML.015:2025 Indirect Prompt Injection GenAI Embedding hidden adversarial instructions in untrusted third-party documents, web pages, or email messages retrieved during inference. NISTAML.018:2025 Direct Prompt Injection GenAI Submitting adversarial conversational prefixes designed to bypass system prompt alignment and override developer guardrails. NISTAML.020:2025 Adversarial Evasion PredAI Adding calculated mathematical perturbations to inference inputs to force classification errors without human-perceptible distortion. NISTAML.025:2025 Supply Chain Deserialization PredAI & GenAI Distributing weaponized weight checkpoints using unsafe execution-capable formats like Python pickle that run arbitrary operating system commands upon loading. NISTAML.031:2025 Model Extraction PredAI & GenAI Submitting targeted query distributions to reconstruct proprietary model weights, decision boundaries, or tokenizer logic. NISTAML.033:2025 Membership Inference PredAI & GenAI Querying models to statistically verify whether specific confidential records were present in the training corpus. NISTAML.040:2025 Sponge Attacks GenAI Submitting crafted token sequences that trigger pathological computation cycles, exhausting host GPU memory and degrading throughput.

docs.title: Integration With NIST AI RMF 1.0
docs.text:
The 2025 standard bridges adversarial machine learning with broader enterprise governance by mapping specific technical mitigations directly to the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (NIST AI 100-1) core functions:

  1. Govern: Establishing policies that prohibit the unverified deployment of external open-source weights and mandating secure model registries.
  2. Map: Identifying whether application components interact with untrusted external text, untrusted third-party APIs, or unverified RAG vector stores.
  3. Measure: Benchmarking models against automated adversarial suites (evaluating empirical evasion rates, prompt extraction success rates, and token consumption bounds).
  4. Manage: Implementing defense-in-depth controls, including context delimiter isolation, input perplexity filtering, runtime guardrails, and cryptographic artifact signing.

docs.title: Role in Purple Teaming
docs.text:
Purple teams use the machine-readable NISTAML catalog from NIST AI 100-2 E2025 to index automated adversarial test suites and track defensive coverage. Because the 2025 specification separates Predictive AI from Generative AI, the Red Team tailors test playbooks to the exact model modality—executing mathematical evasion attacks (NISTAML.020:2025) against classification services or direct prompt injections (NISTAML.018:2025) against language models.

This standardized indexing connects offensive findings directly to enterprise risk metrics under the NIST AI RMF. When the Red Team executes an attack, Blue engineers verify whether detection rules and inference guardrails tag the event with the corresponding NISTAML identifier in security information and event management (SIEM) systems. This collaborative mapping validates the Measure and Manage functions of the AI risk framework, allowing teams to track mitigation progress across specific attack classes and verify that defenses withstand recurring exploitation attempts.

docs.title: Mapping to SCF C|P-RMM
docs.text: The structured classification in NIST AI 100-2 E2025 maps into the SCF C|P-RMM model by connecting machine-readable attack codes with organizational control gaps and operational harm.

docs.title: 1. NISTAML Techniques as Threats
docs.text: In SCF C|P-RMM, a Threat is the person or entity capable of causing damage. The NISTAML identifiers formally define the specific manifestations of that threat. An attacker executing an indirect prompt injection (NISTAML.015:2025) or a data poisoning campaign (NISTAML.010:2025) acts as the active threat agent.

docs.title: 2. Systemic Weaknesses as Control Deficiencies
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, a Vulnerability is defined as a Control Deficiency (an absent, failing, or inadequately configured defensive mechanism).

NIST AI 100-2 E2025 identifies the architectural control failures that allow NISTAML threats to succeed: * Ingesting user-supplied documents into an LLM context without delimiter enforcement represents an input boundary control deficiency. * Loading model checkpoints serialized with pickle instead of Safetensors represents a software supply chain integrity control deficiency. * Deploying unmonitored model endpoints without rate limiting represents an availability and resource governance deficiency.

docs.title: 3. Operational Outcomes as Realized Risk
docs.text:
In SCF C|P-RMM, Risk is the business impact produced when a threat exploits a control deficiency (\(\text{Risk} = \text{Threat} \times \text{Vulnerability} \times \text{Impact}\)).

NIST AI 100-2 E2025 aligns these impacts with core enterprise risk classes: * Integrity Risk: Flawed automated decision-making, compromised legal analysis, or biased diagnostic models resulting from prompt manipulation or data poisoning. * Confidentiality Risk: Unauthorized disclosure of internal system prompts, customer database entries, or proprietary source code through training data extraction (NISTAML.031:2025). * Availability Risk: Service outages, degraded response latency, and excessive cloud computing expenses caused by sponge attacks (NISTAML.040:2025).

docs.title: Critique
docs.text:
The release of NIST AI 100-2 E2025 marks a major step forward for ML security by introducing the NISTAML identification taxonomy. In traditional cybersecurity, vulnerability management depends on shared catalogs like MITRE ATT&CK, CWE, and CVE. By assigning standardized codes to adversarial machine learning techniques, E2025 gives security operations teams a common language to index incident logs, track automated red team findings, and configure detection rules.

Furthermore, the explicit separation between Predictive AI and Generative AI resolves the confusion that plagued earlier frameworks, where traditional statistical attacks (like gradient-based evasion) were often conflated with natural language manipulation (like jailbreaking).

However, organizations adopting NIST AI 100-2 E2025 must manage a practical operational transition:

Because the NISTAML identification schema was finalized in 2025, commercial security tooling, vulnerability databases, and existing regulatory audits are still transitioning away from the prose section numbers used in the 2023 edition. Security teams must maintain cross-reference mappings between legacy citations (such as Section 3.3.1) and current identifiers (NISTAML.018:2025) during this transitional phase.

---
